summary.text: For odd prime \(p\), Fermat’s theorem gives \(2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\); after splitting the shifted sum, every new initial term vanishes because its product contains \(2^{2(p-1)}-1\), while the remaining terms match termwise using periodicity of the product factors and \(\binom{k+2(p-1)+1}{2}-\binom{k+1}{2}=(p-1)(2k+2p-1)\). For \(p=2\), all terms except \(k=0\) vanish modulo \(2\), so every positive-indexed value is congruent to \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_k=\frac{k(k+1)}2=\binom{k+1}{2}.
\]
Thus, with the convention that a product over an empty set is equal to \(1\), the sequence is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_k}\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
We prove that for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

We first dispose of the prime \(p=2\). Let \(m\geq1\). In the summand with \(k=0\), the power of two is
\[
2^{T_0}=2^0=1.
\]
Every index in the accompanying product satisfies \(j\geq1\), and hence \(2^j-1\) is odd. Therefore the entire \(k=0\) summand is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2\). On the other hand, if \(k\geq1\), then \(T_k=k(k+1)/2>0\), so \(2^{T_k}\) is even. Every such summand is consequently \(0\) modulo \(2\). It follows that
\[
a(m)\equiv1\pmod2
\]
for every \(m\geq1\). In particular, both \(n\) and \(n+2(2-1)=n+2\) are positive, so
\[
a(n+2)\equiv a(n)\pmod2.
\]
This proves the assertion for \(p=2\).

Now suppose that \(p\) is an odd prime, and put
\[
r=p-1.
\]
Since \(p\nmid2\), Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^r\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
It follows in particular that
\[
2^{2r}=(2^r)^2\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
We shall evaluate \(a(n+2r)\) modulo \(p\) and divide its summands into two blocks.

By definition,
\[
a(n+2r)=\sum_{K=0}^{n+2r-1}2^{T_K}
             \prod_{j=K+1}^{n+2r-1}(2^j-1).
\]
First consider an index \(K\) with \(0\leq K<2r\). Then \(K+1\leq2r\). Also, because \(n\geq1\),
\[
2r\leq n+2r-1.
\]
Thus \(j=2r\) occurs among the indices in the product
\(
\prod_{j=K+1}^{n+2r-1}(2^j-1).
\)
The corresponding factor is \(2^{2r}-1\), which is \(0\) modulo \(p\) by (1). Hence every summand in the first block \(0\leq K<2r\) vanishes modulo \(p\). Therefore, after writing the remaining indices uniquely as \(K=2r+k\), where \(0\leq k<n\), we obtain
\[
a(n+2r)\equiv
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_{2r+k}}
       \prod_{j=2r+k+1}^{2r+n-1}(2^j-1)
       \pmod p. \tag{2}
\]

We next show that, for each \(k\) in this last sum, its summand is congruent to the \(k\)-th summand of \(a(n)\).

For the initial power of two, direct expansion of the triangular numbers gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{2r+k}
 &=\frac{(2r+k)(2r+k+1)}2\\
 &=\frac{k(k+1)}2+r(2k+2r+1)\\
 &=T_k+r(2k+2r+1).
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
Using \(2^r\equiv1\pmod p\), equation (3) yields
\[
2^{T_{2r+k}}
 =2^{T_k}\bigl(2^r\bigr)^{2k+2r+1}
 \equiv2^{T_k}\pmod p. \tag{4}
\]

Now consider the product in the same summand. Translate its index by writing
\[
j=2r+\ell.
\]
As \(j\) runs from \(2r+k+1\) through \(2r+n-1\), the new index \(\ell\) runs from \(k+1\) through \(n-1\). Moreover, for every such \(\ell\),
\[
2^{2r+\ell}=2^\ell(2^r)^2\equiv2^\ell\pmod p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{2r+\ell}-1\equiv2^\ell-1\pmod p,
\]
and multiplying these congruences over the translated interval gives
\[
\prod_{j=2r+k+1}^{2r+n-1}(2^j-1)
\equiv
\prod_{\ell=k+1}^{n-1}(2^\ell-1)
\pmod p. \tag{5}
\]
This also covers the case \(k=n-1\), when both products are empty and hence equal to \(1\).

Multiplying (4) and (5), we find for every \(0\leq k<n\) that
\[
2^{T_{2r+k}}
\prod_{j=2r+k+1}^{2r+n-1}(2^j-1)
\equiv
2^{T_k}\prod_{\ell=k+1}^{n-1}(2^\ell-1)
\pmod p. \tag{6}
\]
Substituting (6) into (2) and summing over \(k=0,\ldots,n-1\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+2r)
&\equiv \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{T_k}
       \prod_{\ell=k+1}^{n-1}(2^\ell-1)\\
&=a(n)
\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, \(r=p-1\), so this is exactly
\[
\boxed{a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p}.
\]
The argument applies to every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq1\), as required.
